evidence.label: A Complete Local Domain without a Small Cohen–Macaulay Module

headline: A three-dimensional complete local domain over the complex numbers has no small Cohen–Macaulay module.
scope: The example is one ring in dimension three, built over the complex numbers. It answers the domain form of the question, not every related form.
plain: In algebra, a local ring is a number system that zooms in on one point of a shape. Melvin Hochster asked in the early 1970s whether every complete local domain has a small Cohen–Macaulay module, a finite and very well-behaved module. This paper claims to build a three-dimensional example that has none. The ring comes from a cone over one carefully chosen curved surface.
doesNot: This does not rule out the infinite (big) Cohen–Macaulay modules, which are known to exist.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles a question from Hochster's early work that later homological work kept returning to.

explanation:
Start with a test that uses only multiplication. The paper builds one curved surface for each prime n of 3 or more. Each surface comes with two whole numbers. The first is 5n³. The second is n³(n² − 10). The paper's test asks whether the second number is at most six times the first.

Try n = 3. The numbers are 135 and −27, and −27 is far below 6 × 135 = 810. The test passes. Try n = 5. The numbers are 625 and 1,875, and 1,875 is below 3,750. It passes again. Now try n = 7. The numbers are 1,715 and 13,377, while six times 1,715 is 10,290. The test fails, and that failure is the whole counterexample.

To see why, some words are needed. A ring is a number system where you can add and multiply. A local ring zooms in on a single point of a shape, the way power series zoom in on zero. Complete means infinite power series are allowed. A domain is a ring where two nonzero things never multiply to zero. A module over a ring is like a vector space whose scalars come from that ring.

Depth measures how well a module behaves. Pick elements of the ring one by one, so that multiplying by each one never sends a nonzero part of the module to zero. Depth is the longest such run. A small Cohen–Macaulay module is a nonzero module built from finitely many generators whose depth equals the dimension of the ring. The domain form of the conjecture asks whether every complete local domain has one[1].

Melvin Hochster raised this question in his early work[2]. His first paper on it appeared in 1973. In dimension one or two the answer is yes[3]. If infinitely many generators are allowed, so-called big Cohen–Macaulay modules exist, by work running from Hochster in 1975 to André in 2018. In 2014, Bhargav Bhatt found rings with no finite Cohen–Macaulay extension ring[4]. That ruled out one route, but not general modules. Hochster later wrote that he had come to expect counterexamples[5].

This paper claims a counterexample in dimension three[6]. The ring R is built from a cone over a surface. Take all polynomial-like functions on the surface, graded by degree, and zoom in on the tip of the cone. The paper claims R has no nonzero finite module of depth three. It also gives an uncompleted version, essentially defined by finitely many polynomial equations, with the same property[7].

The engine is an inequality[8]. If the cone ring over a surface has a small Cohen–Macaulay module, the surface must pass the test. The surfaces come from six lines through four points of the plane, followed by a branched covering[9]. For n = 7 the test fails, so the cone ring has no such module[10].

The one obstacle is that a module over the completed ring need not respect degrees[12]. Earlier inequalities of this kind worked only for graded modules or special sheaves on the surface. The paper keeps the module's actual geometry near the tip instead. It compares two ways of extending that geometry across the surface sitting at the tip. Then Bogomolov's classical inequality supplies the upper bound that clashes with the test[13].

The work also overlaps with two recent preprints. One excludes graded modules over the same rings. Another, by Chen, proposes a similar completed counterexample by a different bound. The paper says its existence claim overlaps with that work[14].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked only part of it. Lean confirms that a ring with the stated basic properties exists. Lean does not check that the ring lacks a small Cohen–Macaulay module. So the main claim rests on the paper's own argument. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proof holds. Lean checks only the basic properties of the ring, not the missing module. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A number system that zooms in on one point, with a single maximal ideal.
Here, a local ring in which infinite power series in its elements make sense.
A ring where two nonzero elements never multiply to zero.
Something like a vector space, but with scalars taken from a ring.
The longest run of ring elements that each act on the module without killing any nonzero part.
A nonzero, finitely generated module whose depth equals the ring's dimension.
A classical bound on the numbers attached to well-balanced vector bundles on a surface.
